claim: C. elegans feeds in large groups on ephemeral bacterial patches growing on decomposing plant material.
source: C. elegans feeds in large groups on ephemeral bacterial patches growing on decomposing plant material, a habitat that can be mimicked in a petri dish (Frézal and Félix, 2015; Schulenburg and Félix, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Frézal and Félix, 2015; Schulenburg and Félix, 2017).

claim: C. elegans can evaluate population density inside food patches using a suite of pheromones belonging to the family of ascarosides.
source: C. elegans can evaluate population density inside food patches using a suite of pheromones, belonging to the family of ascarosides, which are continuously excreted by worms (Greene et al., 2016; Ludewig and Schroeder, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Greene et al., 2016; Ludewig and Schroeder, 2013).

claim: Ascaroside pheromones are continuously excreted by C. elegans worms.
source: C. elegans can evaluate population density inside food patches using a suite of pheromones, belonging to the family of ascarosides, which are continuously excreted by worms (Greene et al., 2016; Ludewig and Schroeder, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Greene et al., 2016; Ludewig and Schroeder, 2013).

claim: Pheromones and food availability control the leaving times of foraging C. elegans worms.
source: Finally, it has been shown that pheromones and food availability control the leaving times of foraging worms.
evidence: This claim is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The rate at which C. elegans individuals abandon a food patch increases when food becomes scarce and pheromones are at high concentrations.
source: In particular, the rate at which individuals abandon the patch increases when food becomes scarce and pheromones are at high concentrations (Figure 1A; Harvey, 2009; Milward et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Harvey, 2009; Milward et al., 2011) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Individual C. elegans worms leave a food patch at different times during the feeding process.
source: In agreement with previous results (Milward et al., 2011), we found that feeding animals abandon the food patch at very different times, with some worms leaving at the beginning while others staying until the food patch is depleted (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and citation to previous work (Milward et al., 2011).

claim: C. elegans worms leaving a food patch early (first three hours) are attracted to the pheromone blend.
source: In addition, the leaving time affects worms' preference for their pheromones, with individuals leaving the food patch early (first three hours) going to the pheromone blend (positive chemotaxis index, Figure 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: C. elegans worms leaving a food patch later avoid the pheromone blend.
source: while worms leaving the food patch later avoiding it (negative chemotaxis index, Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The leaving time from a food patch affects C. elegans preference for pheromones.
source: In addition, the leaving time affects worms' preference for their pheromones, with individuals leaving the food patch early (first three hours) going to the pheromone blend (positive chemotaxis index, Figure 1D) while worms leaving the food patch later avoiding it (negative chemotaxis index, Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: C. elegans responses to food depletion include an inversion in pheromone preference dependent on the leaving time from the food patch.
source: C. elegans responses to food depletion, therefore, include an inversion in pheromone preference dependent on the leaving time from the food patch.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing different pheromone preferences at different leaving times.

claim: Bacterial food is patchily distributed inside rotting fruits and stems where C. elegans forage.
source: Inside rotting fruits and stems where C. elegans forage, bacterial food is patchily distributed (Frézal and Félix, 2015; Schulenburg and Félix, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Frézal and Félix, 2015; Schulenburg and Félix, 2017).

claim: The timing of dispersal from existing food patches is crucial for C. elegans survival.
source: We might then expect that the timing of dispersal from existing food patches and the strategies that optimize food intake are crucial for worm survival.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the patchy distribution of food.

claim: The inversion in pheromone preference can be an adaptive solution to optimize food intake during foraging in C. elegans.
source: We further demonstrate that the inversion from attraction to repulsion depends on associative learning and, by implementing a simple model, we highlight that it is an adaptive solution to optimize food intake during foraging.
evidence: This claim is supported by the theoretical model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The theoretical model uses Game Theory to find the strategy that maximizes food eaten by a worm.
source: This model uses the tools of Game Theory to find the strategy that maximizes the food eaten by a worm, taking into account that other worms will also follow the same strategy.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology of the theoretical model.

claim: The Evolutionary Stable Strategy should have been selected by evolution.
source: This strategy is called Evolutionary Stable Strategy, and should have been selected by evolution (Maynard Smith, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Game Theory literature (Maynard Smith, 1982).

claim: Unoccupied food patches are hard to find because they are not marked by pheromones and may be on average further away.
source: We assume that unoccupied food patches are hard to find, because they are not marked by pheromones and may be on average further away.
evidence: This is an assumption stated in the theoretical model.

claim: Dispersal will not be advantageous until the occupied food patches are nearly depleted.
source: Therefore, dispersal will not be advantageous until the occupied food patches are nearly depleted.
evidence: This claim is derived from the model assumptions and resembles the marginal value theorem.

claim: When switching is costless, all worms should switch in order to perfectly equalize their distribution across the two food patches.
source: The difference between the two payoffs diminishes as the probability of switching increases, but if switching is costless all worms should switch in order to perfectly equalize their distribution across the two food patches (Figure 2B, blue).
evidence: This claim is derived from the theoretical model and illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: When switching is costly, the equilibrium is reached when only a fraction of the population switches.
source: In contrast, when switching is costly, the equilibrium is reached when only a fraction of the population switches (Figure 2B orange).
evidence: This claim is derived from the theoretical model and illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: The equilibrium fraction of worms that switch depends both on the cost of switching and on the initial imbalance in patch occupancy.
source: This equilibrium fraction (p*) depends both on the cost of switching and on the initial imbalance in patch occupancy (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is derived from the theoretical model and illustrated in Figure 2C.

claim: A fraction of worms will switch at the beginning, leaving the food patch before it is depleted and following pheromones to reach another occupied food patch.
source: Our model recapitulates the two key experimental observations highlighted in Figure 1: First, a fraction of worms will switch at the beginning, leaving the food patch before it is depleted and following pheromones to reach another occupied food patch.
evidence: This claim is derived from the theoretical model and connects to experimental observations.

claim: Once the food patches are depleted all worms will disperse, avoiding depleted food patches by reversing their preference for pheromones.
source: Second, once the food patches are depleted all worms will disperse, avoiding depleted food patches by reversing their preference for pheromones (which now mark depleted food patches).
evidence: This claim is derived from the theoretical model and connects to experimental observations.

claim: C. elegans worms conditioned with +food +pheromone blend are attracted to the pheromone blend.
source: We found that worms go to the pheromone blend when they are conditioned with +food + pheromone blend whereas they avoid it when they are conditioned with – food +pheromone blend (Figure 3B, blue and yellow bars, chemotaxis index of CI++ = 0.38 ± 0.07 vs CI-+ = – 0.15 ± 0.04).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: C. elegans worms conditioned with -food +pheromone blend avoid the pheromone blend.
source: We found that worms go to the pheromone blend when they are conditioned with +food + pheromone blend whereas they avoid it when they are conditioned with – food +pheromone blend (Figure 3B, blue and yellow bars, chemotaxis index of CI++ = 0.38 ± 0.07 vs CI-+ = – 0.15 ± 0.04).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: C. elegans worms conditioned without the pheromone blend do not exhibit a particular preference for their pheromones.
source: Interestingly, worms conditioned without the pheromone blend do not exhibit a particular preference for their pheromones (Figure 3B, red and turquoise bars, chemotaxis index for the + food – pheromone blend and the – food – pheromone blend scenarios are 0 ± 0.07 and – 0.02 ± 0.06, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: C. elegans exhibit attraction when pheromones are paired with abundant food and aversion when pheromones are associated with absence of food.
source: Worms therefore exhibit attraction when pheromones are paired with abundant food and aversion when pheromones are associated with absence of food.
evidence: This claim summarizes the experimental results from the conditioning experiments.

claim: The findings are consistent with the hypothesis that C. elegans preference for the pheromone blend changes due to associative learning.
source: These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that the C. elegans preference for the pheromone blend changes due to associative learning.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: C. elegans can change its preference for both ascr#5 and icas#9 ascarosides.
source: We found that C. elegans can change its preference for both ascarosides (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that ascaroside pheromones are likely contributing to the response to the pheromone blend found previously.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ascaroside pheromones are likely contributing to the response to the pheromone blend.
source: We found that C. elegans can change its preference for both ascarosides (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that ascaroside pheromones are likely contributing to the response to the pheromone blend found previously.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results with pure ascarosides.

claim: The preference for the pheromone blend is retained in the -repellent +pheromone blend conditioning scenario.
source: We found that the preference for the pheromone blend, which is retained in the – repellent + pheromone blend scenario (Figure 4B, blue bar, CI-+=0.26 ± 0.04), is lost in the + repellent + pheromone blend condition (Figure 4B, yellow bar, CI ++ = 0.04 ± 0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The preference for the pheromone blend is lost in the +repellent +pheromone blend conditioning scenario.
source: We found that the preference for the pheromone blend, which is retained in the – repellent + pheromone blend scenario (Figure 4B, blue bar, CI-+=0.26 ± 0.04), is lost in the + repellent + pheromone blend condition (Figure 4B, yellow bar, CI ++ = 0.04 ± 0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Animals do not exhibit a particular preference for pheromones except when they are exposed to pheromones and food in the absence of the repellent.
source: In other words, animals do not exhibit a particular preference for pheromones, except when they are exposed to pheromones and food (in the absence of the repellent).
evidence: This claim summarizes the experimental results from the repellent conditioning experiments.

claim: Exposure to the repellent in the presence of food and pheromones is required to disrupt attraction.
source: Exposure to the repellent in the presence of food and pheromones is required to disrupt attraction.
evidence: This claim is derived from the experimental results with the repellent.

claim: The outcome of the repellent experiment provides further support that C. elegans can change its preference for the pheromone cocktail through associative learning.
source: The outcome of this experiment provides further support that C. elegans can change its preference for the pheromone cocktail it produces through associative learning.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The inversion from attraction to repulsion depends on associative learning.
source: We showed that this inversion from attraction to repulsion depends on associative learning and appears to be an adaptive solution to optimize food intake during foraging.
evidence: This claim is supported by the conditioning experiments and theoretical model.

claim: The inversion in pheromone preference appears to be an adaptive solution to optimize food intake during foraging.
source: We showed that this inversion from attraction to repulsion depends on associative learning and appears to be an adaptive solution to optimize food intake during foraging.
evidence: This claim is supported by the theoretical model.

claim: A change from pheromone attraction to repulsion is required to optimize food intake when three different factors are combined: food patches that give diminishing returns, competition for limited resources, and non-stationarity.
source: Our model shows that a change from pheromone attraction to repulsion is required to optimize food intake when three different factors are combined. First, food patches that give diminishing returns, and should be abandoned when the environment provides a better average intake rate... The second factor is competition for limited resources... The third key factor in our model is non-stationarity
evidence: This claim is derived from the theoretical model analysis.

claim: The Evolutionary Stable Strategy found by the model does not give any benefit at the level of the species and may even be deleterious.
source: It is interesting to note that the Evolutionary Stable Strategy found by our model does not give any benefit at the level of the species, and may even be deleterious.
evidence: This claim is derived from analysis of the theoretical model.

claim: The Evolutionary Stable Strategy emerges from intraspecific competition.
source: This Evolutionary Stable Strategy therefore emerges from intraspecific competition: Individuals benefit from paying the cost of switching to prevent being outcompeted by other individuals within the population, even if the end result is deleterious for the population as a whole.
evidence: This claim is derived from analysis of the theoretical model.

claim: C. elegans preference for environmental stimuli can change through experience, including acclimation and associative learning phenomena.
source: An important evolutionary adaptation in this regard is that the C. elegans preference for each of these stimuli can change through experience, including acclimation (Fenk and de Bono, 2017) and associative learning phenomena (Ardiel and Rankin, 2010; Colbert and Bargmann, 1995; Rankin, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: During feeding, C. elegans worms learn to give a positive or negative preference to pheromones depending on the context in which they experience them, in particular the presence or absence of food.
source: During feeding, worms learn to give a positive or negative preference to pheromones depending on the context in which they experience them, in particular the presence or absence of food (Wyatt, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results and a citation (Wyatt, 2014).

claim: Experienced bumblebee foragers that learnt to associate chemical footprints with the absence of nectar can successfully avoid marked flowers and increase their overall nectar intake.
source: It has been shown that only experienced foragers, that is those that learnt to associate the chemical footprints with the absence of nectar in marked flowers, can successfully avoid them and increase their overall nectar intake (Ayasse and Jarau, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research (Ayasse and Jarau, 2014).

claim: Associative learning based on pairing pheromones or similar chemical signals with food availability might be frequently observed in animals feeding in groups as a strategy to increase food intake.
source: This suggests that associative learning based on pairing pheromones or similar chemical signals with food availability might be frequently observed in animals feeding in groups, not only eusocial insects, as a strategy to increase food intake.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the bumblebee example and the C. elegans results.

claim: Dispersal of feeding stages of C. elegans from occupied patches is regulated by the recent experience of food availability and pheromones.
source: We have shown that dispersal of feeding stages of C. elegans from occupied patches is regulated by the recent experience of food availability and pheromones, which indicates, at any time, whether it is better to follow the scent of pheromones or to avoid it.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main experimental findings.

claim: A mechanism based on the synergistic interaction between food and pheromones regulates C. elegans dispersal over longer time scales and its boom-and-bust life cycle.
source: A mechanism based on the synergistic interaction between food and pheromones also regulates C. elegans dispersal over longer time scales and, in general, its boom-and-bust life cycle (Edison, 2009; Frézal and Félix, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Edison, 2009; Frézal and Félix, 2015).

claim: Scarce food and high concentration of pheromones promote the entry into the dauer larva stage in C. elegans.
source: Indeed, scarce food and high concentration of pheromones promote the entry into a resting stage (the dauer larva), allowing worms to survive unfavorable seasons and disperse to uncolonized rotten material, where abundant food, in turn, resumes development to adulthood (Frézal and Félix, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research (Frézal and Félix, 2015).

claim: Abundant food resumes development to adulthood in C. elegans after the dauer stage.
source: Indeed, scarce food and high concentration of pheromones promote the entry into a resting stage (the dauer larva), allowing worms to survive unfavorable seasons and disperse to uncolonized rotten material, where abundant food, in turn, resumes development to adulthood (Frézal and Félix, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research (Frézal and Félix, 2015).

claim: Non-dauer stages play an important role in exploiting transient bacterial patches in C. elegans.
source: Our findings establish an interesting parallel between mechanisms promoting dispersal over short and long temporal scales and highlight the important role that non-dauer stages play in exploiting transient bacterial patches.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Ascr#5 and icas#9 are potent signaling cues that are usually detected in C. elegans exudates.
source: Ascr#5 and icas#9 are potent signaling cues that are usually detected in C. elegans exudates (von Reuss et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research (von Reuss et al., 2012).

claim: The list of newly discovered compounds of the worm metabolism acting as signaling molecules is continuously expanding.
source: but other ascarosides can be abundant and the list of newly discovered compounds of the worm metabolism acting as signaling molecules is continuously expanding (von Reuss et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research (von Reuss et al., 2012).

claim: The composition of the pheromone blend varies among developmental stages in C. elegans.
source: More studies are required to establish a link between associative learning and the composition of the pheromone blend, which is known to vary among developmental stages (Kaplan et al., 2011), sexes (Izrayelit et al., 2012) and strains (Diaz et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research (Kaplan et al., 2011).

claim: The composition of the pheromone blend varies among sexes in C. elegans.
source: More studies are required to establish a link between associative learning and the composition of the pheromone blend, which is known to vary among developmental stages (Kaplan et al., 2011), sexes (Izrayelit et al., 2012) and strains (Diaz et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research (Izrayelit et al., 2012).

claim: The composition of the pheromone blend varies among strains in C. elegans.
source: More studies are required to establish a link between associative learning and the composition of the pheromone blend, which is known to vary among developmental stages (Kaplan et al., 2011), sexes (Izrayelit et al., 2012) and strains (Diaz et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research (Diaz et al., 2014).

claim: C. elegans preference for pheromones might not be innate.
source: As a final remark, our results suggest that C. elegans preference for pheromones might not be innate, as it was previously stated (Greene et al., 2016; Macosko et al., 2009; Pungaliya et al., 2009; Simon and Sternberg, 2002; Srinivasan et al., 2012; Srinivasan et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and contrasts with previous literature.

claim: The attraction that 'naive' worms exhibit may be due to the positive association with food that they learn to make during growth on the plate.
source: Hence, it is possible that the attraction that 'naive' worms exhibit is due to the positive association with food that they learn to make during growth on the plate.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The social behavior of the canonical lab strain N2 has changed due to laboratory domestication.
source: Thus, it remains to be tested if the same responses occur in the canonical lab strain N2, whose social behavior has changed due to laboratory domestication (Sterken et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research (Sterken et al., 2015).

claim: The MY1 strain was used to assess behavioral patterns that could be as close as possible to those exhibited by C. elegans in its natural habitat.
source: We used young adult hermaphrodites of the natural isolate MY1 (Lingen, Germany) to assess behavioral patterns that could be as close as possible to those exhibited by C. elegans in its natural habitat.
evidence: This claim explains the rationale for strain selection.

claim: The pheromone blend is obtained by collecting and filtering the supernatant of well-fed worms maintained in a liquid culture.
source: In these experiments, the pheromone blend is obtained by collecting and filtering the supernatant of well-fed worms maintained in a liquid culture (Choe et al., 2012; Harvey, 2009; White et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methodology and is supported by citations.

claim: Foraging for food is among the most critical activities for an animal's survival.
source: Foraging for food is among the most critical activities for an animal's survival (Calhoun et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research (Calhoun et al., 2014).

claim: Food is usually patchily distributed in space and time.
source: It is also among the most challenging, because food is usually patchily distributed in space and time, and other individuals are attempting to find and consume the same resources (Abu Baker and Brown, 2014; Driessen and Bernstein, 1999; Stephens and Krebs, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Foragers are predicted to depart from a food patch when the instantaneous intake rate drops below the average intake rate expected from the environment.
source: As such, foragers are predicted to depart from a food patch when the instantaneous intake rate drops below the average intake rate expected from the environment, a phenomenon that has been observed in several animals, from insects (Wajnberg et al., 2008) to birds (Cowie, 1977; Krebs et al., 1974) and large mammals (Searle et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research across multiple taxa.

claim: The presence of other animals affects individual foraging success so that different leaving times can be expected.
source: The presence of other animals, however, affects individual foraging success so that different leaving times can be expected (Aubert-Kato et al., 2015; Couzin et al., 2005; Giraldeau and Caraco, 2000; Karpas et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Animals use pheromones and other odors to orientate their searches for food.
source: Since natural habitats are usually saturated with many different non-specific chemical cues, animals use pheromones and other odors to orientate their searches (Wyatt, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research (Wyatt, 2014).

claim: In the context of social foraging, individuals might need to rely only on the most recent experience.
source: In the context of social foraging, it has been shown that individuals might need to rely only on the most recent experience (Krebs and Inman, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research (Krebs and Inman, 1992).

claim: The valence of pheromones acquired during the most recent feeding activity is crucial for the success of the foraging process.
source: As such, the valence (positive or negative signal) of pheromones acquired during the most recent feeding activity is crucial for the success of the foraging process.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the discussion of social foraging and recent experience.

claim: Ascaroside pheromones are likely contributing to foraging optimization in C. elegans.
source: We found that C. elegans can change its preference for both ascarosides (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that ascaroside pheromones are likely contributing to the response to the pheromone blend found previously. However, these experiments were performed at high worm density, meaning that accumulation of secreted pheromones during the conditioning period prevents a definitive quantification of the relative importance of associative learning versus feeding status (as in Figure 3 inset with the pheromone blend). Nonetheless, these results show that C. elegans can alter its preference for ascarosides, highlighting the flexible role of pheromones in foraging optimization.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results with pure ascarosides.

claim: The pheromone blend contains ascaroside pheromones, other products of worm metabolism, compounds deriving from the decomposition of dead worms and bacteria, and perhaps other unknown substances.
source: In addition to a cocktail of ascaroside pheromones, the pheromone blend contains other products of worm metabolism, compounds deriving from the decomposition of dead worms and bacteria, and perhaps other unknown substances.
evidence: This claim describes the composition of the pheromone blend used in experiments.

claim: Worms could learn and change preference for any of the compounds in the pheromone blend and thus forage efficiently.
source: Worms could in principle learn and change preference for any of these compounds and thus forage efficiently as indicated by our model.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the model predictions.

claim: Sodium azide is used to anesthetize C. elegans in the behavioral assays.
source: In the pheromone and control spots, 2 μl of 0.5 M sodium azide was added in order to anesthetize the animals once they reached the spots.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methodology.

claim: The anesthetic action of sodium azide lasts for about 2 hr in the choice after food assay setup.
source: Since the anesthetic action of sodium azide lasts for about 2 hr in this set-up, another 1 μl was added two hours after the beginning of the assay in both spots.
evidence: This claim describes an observation about the experimental methodology.

claim: The MY1 strain was obtained from the Caenorhabditis Genetic Centre (CGC).
source: The strain has been obtained from the Caenorhabditis Genetic Centre (CGC).
evidence: This claim describes the source of the experimental strain.

claim: A new pheromone blend was produced every 3 months for the experiments.
source: A new pheromone blend was produced every 3 months.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methodology.

claim: The control solvent for the pheromone blend is S-medium.
source: The control solvent for the pheromone blend is S-medium, while the control solvent for the pure ascarosides is an aqueous solution with the same amount of ethanol present in the ascaroside aqueous solution (Srinivasan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methodology.

claim: The control solvent for pure ascarosides is an aqueous solution with the same amount of ethanol present in the ascaroside aqueous solution.
source: The control solvent for the pheromone blend is S-medium, while the control solvent for the pure ascarosides is an aqueous solution with the same amount of ethanol present in the ascaroside aqueous solution (Srinivasan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methodology and is supported by citation.
